opus-5.5.text:
Because if your idea survives all the way to the paper exactly as you first imagined it, it usually means you didn't learn anything along the way. Research is supposed to be a process of discovery. You start with a hypothesis, you run experiments, and the world pushes back. Something doesn't work the way you expected, some result surprises you, and that surprise is where the real insight lives. If nothing ever surprised you, then either the idea was so obvious that someone could have predicted the outcome without doing the work, or you weren't really listening to what the experiments were telling you.

I see this a lot, especially with students. They come in with a plan, almost like an engineering spec: "I'm going to build this module, add it to this architecture, and get two points on this benchmark." Then they execute it, and sometimes it even works. But the paper ends up being incremental. It's a confirmation of what they already believed, and the community doesn't gain much from it.

The best projects I've been part of look very different at the end than at the beginning. You start out trying to solve problem A, and halfway through you realize the real question is B, something more fundamental you didn't even know to ask. That pivot is painful, because you have to let go of what you were attached to. But that's the sign you're actually doing research rather than just executing a plan.

So when I say it's the worst kind, I don't mean it's wrong or useless. I mean it misses the point of what research is for. A good researcher should be humble enough to let the data change their mind, and curious enough to follow it somewhere unexpected. If your final paper reads exactly like your first proposal, you probably played it too safe.

r001.rationale: The response says an unchanged idea suggests the researcher learned nothing or that the idea was obvious, but it does not clearly argue that the idea itself was uninteresting.

r002.rationale: The response describes students executing planned projects and producing incremental papers, but does not argue that repeatedly implementing a clever trick yields little cumulative growth for the researcher.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the word "worst" sounds a bit strong, but I do mean it in a specific sense. If you start a project with an idea, and six months or a year later the paper you publish is exactly that idea, with the same hypothesis, the same method, the same story you had on day one, then something is off. It means the process didn't teach you anything. You were essentially executing a plan, not doing research.

To me, research is about the surprise. You go into a problem with some belief, you run experiments, and the results push back on you. Maybe the thing you thought would matter doesn't matter at all. Maybe a baseline you threw in as a sanity check turns out to be the real finding. That friction between what you expected and what the data says is where new understanding comes from. If there is no friction, either the question was too easy, or you weren't looking carefully, or you were only seeking confirmation.

A lot of my own work has gone that way. ConvNeXt is a good example. We didn't set out to prove convolutions were still great. We started by trying to understand why Transformers worked so well in vision, and we kept modernizing the ConvNet step by step to see where the gap actually was. The conclusion emerged from that process. It wasn't the hypothesis at the beginning. Same with the work on diffusion and representation learning. We went in with one story and the experiments told a different one, and the different one was much more interesting.

So when I talk to students, I tell them: if you're not updating your beliefs during the project, be worried. The initial idea should be a starting point, not a destination. The paper you eventually write should be, in some sense, something you could not have written when you started. That's the whole point of doing the experiments. Otherwise it's just a demo of something you already decided was true, and the community gets a result, but nobody, including you, really learned anything.

r001.rationale: The response says an unchanged project suggests the process taught the researcher nothing, but it does not say the initial idea was uninteresting.

r002.rationale: The response describes executing a plan without learning, but does not connect repeatedly implementing a clever trick for publication with little cumulative growth.

astra-6.text:
Because if the idea stays exactly the same from beginning to end, what did you actually learn along the way? You started with a belief, ran some experiments, and ended up telling the same story. I worry that in that process, you might have treated the experiments as a way to confirm your idea rather than a way to challenge it.

For me, the interesting part of research is that feedback loop. You have an intuition, you try something, and the results surprise you. Then you have to ask whether your assumptions were wrong, whether you were asking the right question, or whether there’s something more interesting hiding in the failure. That should change your thinking.

Of course, an initial idea can be right. But the goal isn’t to protect that idea until it becomes a paper. The goal is to understand something you didn’t understand before. Sometimes the most valuable outcome is realizing that the question you started with wasn’t the important one.

r001.rationale: The response says an unchanged idea suggests little learning and may mean the researcher missed a more interesting question, but it does not argue that the idea itself was uninteresting.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss repeatedly implementing a clever trick for publication or the resulting cumulative growth of the researcher.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if the idea stays exactly the same from the beginning to the final paper, what did you actually learn along the way? You had a belief, and then you spent months finding evidence to support it. That can become an exercise in confirmation rather than discovery.

To me, the initial idea is a starting point. You run experiments, something doesn’t work, or something works for a reason you didn’t expect. Those surprises should change your understanding, and sometimes they should change the question itself. That’s where the interesting research happens.

I’m exaggerating a little when I call it the worst kind of research. A clean initial idea can certainly be right. But I would worry if we treated preserving that idea as the goal. The goal is to understand something better, even if that means the final paper tells a very different story from the one you imagined.

r001.rationale: The response says an unchanged idea risks confirmation rather than discovery, but it does not argue that the idea itself was uninteresting.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss repeatedly implementing a clever trick for publications or the researcher’s cumulative growth.
